upport under sections 4(2) and 4(3) of the 1999 Act is available to failed asylum seekers, individuals whose asylum claims are declared inadmissible under sections 80A or 80B of the Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 and their dependents.

Conditions of support under section 4(2) and 4(3) are governed by regulation 6 of the Immigration and Asylum (Provision of Accommodation to Failed Asylum-Seekers) Regulations 2005 (amended in 2026). Regulation 6(2) status allows the Secretary of State to make the continued provision of accommodation subject to a condition that the person does not engage in illegal working.

Failure to comply with the conditions of support may result in support being suspended or discontinued. For more information see the conditions of support.

Illegal Working Operations Legislation

The legislative framework governing illegal working sets out restrictions on employment, the checks employers must undertake before employing a person subject to immigration control, and the consequences of employing or working without the required permission. The principal provisions are contained in sections 14A to 25 of the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act (IANA) 2006, and the Immigration (Restrictions on Employment) Order 2007.

Section 48 extends the regime beyond traditional employer-employee relationships, including to certain worker, subcontractor and online matching arrangements.

Section 24B of the Immigration Act 1971 sets out the offence of illegal working and section 21 of the Immigration, Asylum and Nationality Act 2006 sets out the offence of employing a migrant who has no right to work.

Actions to take when illegal working is suspected

Where an individual in receipt of section 98, section 95 or section 4 support is suspected of illegal working, a referral should be made to the Asylum Support National Compliance Team. Referrals may be made from different sources, including referrals from Immigration Enforcement.

The evidential threshold that should be applied when investigating illegal working is the balance of probabilities. This aligns with the threshold applied by Immigration Enforcement when investigating illegal working and should apply to those in receipt of section 98, section 95 or section 4 support. A suspicion or allegation of illegal working is not, on its own, sufficient to establish that illegal working has taken place. All available information and evidence should be considered in accordance with the legislative test and procedures in this guidance.

Referrals from Immigration Enforcement

This route will see the Asylum Support National Compliance Team using evidence provided through an Immigration Enforcement investigation into an individual working illegally. The Asylum Support National Compliance Team will then undertake a destitution test prior to discontinuation of support.

Immigration Enforcement officers conduct illegal working operations to identify and investigate employers who knowingly employ an illegal worker, or fail to demonstrate a statutory excuse, meaning they conducted the correct right-to-work checks before employing the individual. These cases are referred to the Civil Penalty Compliance team who can take action against employers, while the Immigration Enforcement investigations can also result in action against individual workers.

Immigration Enforcement Investigations

Immigration Enforcement investigations involve interviews, documentary evidence, and direct observations. This framework is designed to meet a high evidential threshold and support civil penalty action against employers, along with criminal enforcement action where appropriate. Civil penalties are issued by the Civil Penalty Compliance Team.

See also: Illegal working operations

In addition to issuing civil penalties to employers, Immigration Enforcement can identify and enforce illegal working breaches on individual workers if they prove, on the balance of probabilities, that an individual has worked in breach of the conditions of their immigration status or worked without the relevant permission. Their permission may be cancelled, such that they may become liable to administrative removal. To enforce a breach on an individual, there must be firm and recent evidence (normally within 6 months, but this is considered on a case-by-case basis) of working in breach, including at least one of the following:

an admission by the offender of working in breach

a statement by the employer implicating the suspect

documentary evidence such as payslips, the offender’s details on the pay roll, national insurance records, tax records, P45

sight by the Immigration Officer, or by a police officer who gives a statement to that effect, of the offender working, preferably on 2 or more separate occasions, or on one occasion over an extended period, or of wearing the employer’s uniform

In practice, sight only evidence will be insufficient and must be backed up by other evidence.

See also: Initial consideration and assessment of liability to administrative removal

When conducting an illegal working operation, Immigration Enforcement officers may identify an individual in receipt of section 98, section 95 or section 4 support, who they suspect is working without having the right or permission to work. Immigration Enforcement officers should continue to conduct their visit following their usual processes. Once the operation has concluded, referrals from Immigration Enforcement will be sent to the Asylum Support National Compliance Team. The compliance team will be responsible for reviewing these cases and determining if discontinuation of support is appropriate.

escribed by Regulation 4 of the Asylum Seekers (Reception Conditions) Regulations 2005. Compliance officers must consider vulnerabilities on a case-by-case basis and determine if discontinuing support is appropriate based on the evidence they have.

Where a compliance officer decides that discontinuation of support is appropriate following consideration of any vulnerabilities, the Home Office will take reasonable steps to notify the individual that their support has been discontinued in a discontinuation of support letter. This notification will explain that their failure to comply with conditions regarding their right to work has resulted in the discontinuation of their asylum support.

Where evidence of a vulnerability is provided following support being discontinued, compliance officers should reassess whether discontinuation of support remains appropriate based on the evidence provided. If a compliance officer decides that discontinuation is no longer appropriate, support should be reinstated.

When considering whether to discontinue the provision of support under the 1999 Act to families with minors, the course of action taken must be consistent with the Home Office’s obligations under Section 55 of the Borders, Citizenship and Immigration Act 2009, to ensure that the decision has regard to the need to safeguard and promote the welfare of children who are in the UK.

Any decision as to whether it is appropriate to discontinue support must be proportionate to the situation. When making decisions as to whether it would be appropriate to discontinue support for families with minors, compliance officers should consult their senior caseworker before proceeding.

If the discontinuation of support is appropriate, compliance officers should take appropriate steps to safeguard and promote the welfare of the children. Before any action is taken to begin the process to discontinue support, the compliance officer should liaise with the local authority, notifying them that the Home Office plans to discontinue support from the family, and request that the local authority provides alternative support. If the local authority makes an offer of support, the provision of support under Section 98, 95 or 4 should be discontinued as soon as the family transfers into local authority care.

If the Home Office considers that the supported family are eligible for support provided by the local authority, but the local authority refuses to provide support, the provision of asylum support must be maintained until the local authority provides support.

If a decision is taken that it would be appropriate to discontinue the provision of support to a family with children, the discontinuation letter should explain why the decision is consistent with the Home Office’s obligations under Section 55 of the Borders, Citizenship and Immigration Act 2009.

Considerations during the investigation process

Failure to comply with a request

An individual may be asked to attend an interview or provide information during the course of the investigation. An individual will be given a minimum of 5 working days to respond to requests. If the individual fails to comply with this request, support may be suspended to encourage them to comply. If they continue to fail to comply with the request, support may be discontinued.

Failure to Attend an Interview

When a referral of suspected illegal working is received from a source outside of Immigration Enforcement, a compliance officer will complete an investigation to determine if the individual was working illegally. An interview between the individual and the compliance officer may form part of the investigation. Compliance officers will issue a letter to the individual inviting them to attend an interview, which could be face to face or via telephone.

If an individual fails to attend an interview without a reasonable excuse, support may be suspended to encourage compliance. If the individual continues to fail to comply, support should be discontinued on that basis.

Pregnancy

This policy applies to pregnant women, whether or not part of a family group. However, it is recognised that pregnant women may have additional vulnerabilities. Decisions taken to discontinue support for pregnant women will be taken on a case-by-case basis. However, discontinuation will not apply in the late stages of pregnancy, where the Home Office are already aware of the pregnancy. The late stages of pregnancy are defined in the healthcare needs and pregnancy dispersal guidance as normally running from six weeks before the Estimated Date of Delivery (EDD) until a clinician has signed off on the postnatal checks. The latter will usually be around six weeks after birth, unless there have been complications.

Where a pregnancy is raised for the first time in representations made under the policy, this would need to be accompanied by evidence, for example a letter from their treating clinician or a MATB1 form. This guidance should be read alongside the healthcare needs and pregnancy dispersal guidance.

Potential Victims of Modern Slavery

When making a referral to the Asylum Support National Compliance team, the referrer may identify indicators that the individual is a potential victim of modern slavery. If the referrer is a ‘first responder’ they should make a referral into the National Referral Mechanism (NRM).

During a compliance investigation, the compliance officer may identify indicators that raise concerns that the individual has been forced into employment and is a potential victim of modern slavery. For more information on the indicators of modern slavery, compliance officers should refer to the Modern Slavery: Statutory Guidance for England and Wales and Non-Statutory Guidance for Scotland and Northern Ireland.
